lesson.title: The Living -en Suffix
lesson.subtitle: brighten, shorten, deepen — English's own -en verbs are the bridge into German

hook.title: You Use German -en Every Week
hook.content: When English wants to turn an adjective into a verb, it reaches for the Germanic suffix -en: bright → brighten, short → shorten, deep → deepen, wide → widen, hard → harden, dark → darken. You say these without a second thought — and they are, morphologically, German verbs wearing English clothes. German simply never stopped doing what English still does occasionally: every dictionary verb ends in -en. That means the -en shelf of German is not new vocabulary. It is your own suffix, used at full power.

footnotes.title: The Worn-Down Twins
footnotes.content: Three verbs wore their endings down in English but kept them in German: follow lost its g entirely (folgen kept it), wander dropped the -n (wandern kept it), and warn let the -en shrink to nothing (warnen kept it). The German forms are the older shapes of your own words.

pattern.title: One Suffix, Three Strategies
pattern.content: Strategy one — the adjective verb: English brighten works exactly like German's adjective verbs; the suffix means 'make into'. Strategy two — the noun verb: German takes a noun and bolts -en on: Hunger → hungern (to hunger, to be starving). English used to do this too — old texts still say 'they hungered'. Strategy three — the hidden suffix: follow ↔ folgen, wander ↔ wandern, warn ↔ warnen. English chewed the ending off; German serves it whole. Whenever you meet a German verb ending in -ern or -en that begins like an English verb, you already know it.

footnotes.title: The g Inside follow
footnotes.content: folgen and follow descend from the same Proto-Germanic *fulgāną. Old English was folgian — with the g. Middle English wore it into 'folwen', and the modern w is all that remains of the ancient g. German wrote the g down and never let go.

pattern.linguist_note: German also runs a variant -ern (wandern, ändern), from the same West Germanic derivational family. English 'wander' descends from the same root as wandern — the -n tail dropped in the crossing.

exercises.prompt: English 'wander' + the tail German kept = the German verb:
exercises.explanation: wander + -n = wandern. English dropped the final -n; German never did.

exercises.prompt: Match the worn-down English verbs with their full German forms:
exercises.meaning: to follow, to wander, to warn, to hunger
exercises.explanation: English chewed the suffix down; German serves each verb with its full Germanic ending.

exercises.prompt: What English verb shares the exact root of 'folgen'?
exercises.explanation: Both descend from Proto-Germanic *fulgāną — the g in folgen survives as the w of follow.

exercises.prompt: Complete the pronoun × -en verb matrix for 'we sing':
exercises.row_law: Row: subject pronoun (ich takes -e, wir takes -en)
exercises.explanation: With 'wir', the verb keeps the full -en infinitive ending: wir singen, wir finden, wir wandern. [Ref: warnen]

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "We sing and we wander"
exercises.explanation: Same pattern as the First Sentences Gym — the new verb slots straight into the old frame.
cues: Start with "Wir" and anchor "singen" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Derive German -en/-ern verbs from their English twins and use them in wir-sentences.
summary.takeaway: English still coins verbs with Germanic -en (brighten, shorten); German uses that same suffix on every verb — including follow, wander, warn and hunger.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the modal auxiliaries & the bracket — ich will means I want, not the future, and the frame they build.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from The Living -en Suffix (We sing and we wander):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wir singen und wir wandern" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of The Living -en Suffix without relying on short-term echo.

folgen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fulgāną — English softened the ancient g into w (follow), German kept it spelled out. Takes the dative. [wiktionary]

wandern.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn — German kept the full -ern ending that English wore down to -er. [wiktionary]

warnen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *warnōn — a parallel formation to English warn (Old English wearnian). [wiktionary]

hungern.etymology_derivation: Denominal verb from Hunger; English kept "to hunger" in older texts ("they hungered"). [wiktionary]

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

singen.etymology_derivation: Initial S voiced to [z] before vowels.

japan.etymology_derivation: Via Dutch Japan from Malay Jepang, from Hokkien 日本 "sun origin" — the same route as English. [wiktionary]

land.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *landą — the identical twin of English land. [wiktionary]

magen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *magō 'stomach' — related to English maw. [wiktionary]

dame.etymology_derivation: From French dame, Latin domina — Wiktionary: 'Cognate with English dame'. [wiktionary]

violett.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French violet, the flower name — the page's own derivation; English uses the identical word for the identical flower and color. [wiktionary]

schauer.context_phrase: Ein Schauer kommt, nimm den Regenschirm.
schauer.context_translation: A shower is coming, take the umbrella.
schauer.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *skūrō — the page names English shower as a cognate (English palatalized sk to sh, German kept sch); German Schauer also means a shudder. [wiktionary]

vorher.etymology_derivation: A univerbation of vor 'before' + her 'ago, hither' — literally before-here, an everyday adverb built from two ancient words. [wiktionary]

laden.context_phrase: Der Laden um die Ecke ist billig.
laden.context_translation: The shop around the corner is cheap.
laden.etymology_derivation: Originally the board or shutter of a market stall, then the stall itself — the page notes it is akin to English lath, a thin board. [wiktionary]

handschrift.etymology_derivation: Hand + Schrift — handwriting; Schrift is the noun of schreiben (the scribe family). [wiktionary]
